extracted.intended_audience: EPA, state regulators, electric utilities and their legal counsel, and courts considering challenges to EPA's Section 111(d) Proposed Rule
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/regulatory comment challenging EPA's Proposed Rule under Clean Air Act Section 111(d), arguing statutory, regulatory, and administrative-law limits on how EPA may define BSER, source/source-category, and the role of States. Targets EPA rulemakers, state agencies, regulated utilities, and courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on redefining 'Source' and 'Source Category' to include non-owners/operators
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s Proposed Rule Illegally redefines “Source” and “Source Category” to include activities by entities other than owners or operators of regulated sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act and its regulations define “stationary source” as “any building, structure, facility, or installation which emits or may emit any air pollutant.” Emissions controls under Section 111(d) must apply directly to a single building/structure/facility/installation rather than to a combination/agglomeration of such units. EPA’s portfolio/outside-the-fence approach which sweeps in end-users, non-emitting generators, energy markets, transmission and gas infrastructure, and consumers improperly collapses distinct entities into a single source category, rendering 'source category' a nullity. Citations: 40 C.F.R. §60.2, §60.21, §60.26. Examples: replacing unit-specific standards with requirements to use scythes or to shift transport to rail; EPA cannot assume states will build infrastructure beyond their authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER must be limited to systems of emission reduction demonstrated at individual units (inside-the-fence)
rubrics_metrics.description: BSER must be technological or operational measures that can be implemented at a specific unit; emission standards and reductions must apply to individual units/facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's historical practice in NSPS/EG rulemakings has been to identify unit-specific systems (e.g., MSW landfills: a gas collection system + control device achieving 98% reduction). Section 111(d) and implementing regulations contemplate BSER as unit-applicable 'systems of emission reduction.' Outside-the-fence measures that require changes across multiple facilities are inconsistent with that framework. See prior NSPS/EGs for 13 source categories and examples (citations provided in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on basing BSER on measures requiring coordination across multiple facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may not define BSER based on measures that can only be achieved when multiple facilities operate in coordination (emission averaging, allowance trading, demand-side reductions, re-dispatch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'portfolio approach' and Building Blocks that depend on inter-facility coordination effectively define the entire category of existing electric generating units and consumers as a single source, exceeding statutory/regulatory limits. Such approaches attribute reductions to industry/economy-wide changes rather than reductions achievable at particular installations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced utilization or curtailment is not an acceptable component of BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: Building Blocks that achieve reductions by curtailing or eliminating operations of affected units (i.e., requiring them to run less or shut down) do not constitute a 'best system of emission reduction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BSER must improve an existing source's emission rate or performance, not simply reduce the activity that produces emissions. Requiring reduced utilization would permit EPA to order sources to curtail or cease operations without statutory authority. Historical NSPS (over 68) never required reduced unit utilization. Curtailment can also worsen environmental performance (e.g., heat-rate degradation) and thus is counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA lacks authority to regulate demand-side or end-user behavior as BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may not derive emission reductions from regulation of demand or consumer behavior (e.g., end-user energy efficiency) under Section 111(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Building Block 4, which looks to end-user efficiencies and reductions in electricity demand to claim emission reductions, sits outside EPA's authority because utilities and source owners cannot control consumer behavior. Section 111 authorizes regulation of emissions from existing units, not general societal behavior. The Supreme Court requires clear congressional authorization for such transformative expansions (citing UARG).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-category limits: EPA cannot regulate non-members of the designated source category
rubrics_metrics.description: Even under a permissive reading of BSER, EPA is limited to measures within a distinct source category and cannot base BSER on regulation of generators or users outside that category (e.g., renewables, nuclear, consumers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Proposed Rule's inclusion of renewable generation, nuclear plants, energy markets, and end-users into BSER improperly extends regulation beyond the designated fossil-fuel-fired EGU source category. Such a sweeping definition is unworkable and unlawful because it regulates generation/dispatch/consumption rather than systems of emission reduction applied to designated facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability: invalidity of one Building Block requires court determination and may invalidate entire BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s claim of severability for the Building Blocks does not control; courts apply Alaska Airlines two-prong severability test (congressional intent and functional separability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Building Blocks are interrelated (e.g., reduced operation under Blocks 2–4 undermines heat-rate improvements in Block 1) and EPA set state targets assuming all Blocks will function jointly, courts should find the Blocks not severable. If one Block is invalid, EPA must reassess whether remaining Blocks still constitute BSER and must recalculate state targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 111(d) reserves to States the authority to establish standards of performance for existing sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Section 111(d), EPA must 'prescribe regulations' establishing a procedure under which each State shall submit a plan that 'establishes standards of performance for any existing source'; the States — not EPA — establish those standards and apply them to particular sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's role is to (1) develop procedural regulations paralleling SIP provisions and (2) identify a finite adequately-demonstrated BSER upon which States can rely. EPA cannot pre-determine binding, state-specific standards of performance or set state-wide emission reduction goals that states are unable to alter without contravening the statute's cooperative federalism design. Compare Section 111(b)/(c)/(d) distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA's emission guideline documents under 40 C.F.R. §60.22 are informational, not binding
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory text (40 C.F.R. §60.22) limits EPA to issuing nonbinding 'guideline documents' containing information pertinent to control of designated pollutants from designated facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §60.22(b) expressly frames guideline documents as providing information for State plan development (e.g., endangerment info; description of adequately demonstrated systems; achievable degree of reduction; costs; compliance times; emission guideline reflecting BSER considering cost). EPA's present proposal converts 'guidance' into binding statewide goals without amending the underlying regulations via proper notice-and-comment rulemaking, which would be arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: States must be permitted to apply standards unit-by-unit considering remaining useful life and facility-specific factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 111(d) and implementing regulations permit States, when applying standards to particular sources, to consider remaining useful life and facility-specific factors (e.g., unreasonable cost due to plant age/location/design; physical impossibility; other factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 40 C.F.R. §60.24(f) authorizes States to adopt less stringent standards or longer compliance schedules if the State demonstrates facility-specific reasons (unreasonable cost, physical impossibility, other factors). Determinations require careful, facility-by-facility consideration because EPA lacks the local information needed to make such prudential assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must follow its own regulations and cannot adopt conflicting binding requirements without proper rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may not finalize a rule that conflicts with its existing regulations (i.e., transform guidance into binding limits) without first revising those regulations through proper notice-and-comment rulemaking and explaining the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexplained inconsistency with prior agency practice/rules is arbitrary and capricious (citing cases). If EPA intends to promulgate binding statewide emission reduction targets contrary to §60.22's guidance-only approach, it must first amend the underlying regulations via the ordinary rulemaking process; it has not done so here.
